chunks: "The output LC is a second-order low-pass in the loop, with a double pole at 1 over (2 pi square root of LC ) .
Above that frequency the gain falls at 40 decibels per decade and the phase drops by up to 180°, so it eats most of the phase margin unless the compensation provides lead.
In voltage mode the compensator typically has a Type III network with two zeros placed near the double pole to give phase boost.
L and C set where that pole sits and ESR sets a zero at 1 over (2 pi ESR C) .
A bigger L or C moves the pole down, so the crossover has to come down or the compensation has to be retuned.
How sharp the peak is depends on the damping from load and resistance: at light load the resonance is much sharper, so it's the worst case for stability.
Ceramic capacitors have tiny ESR, so their zero is far above crossover and gives no phase boost; electrolytics with higher ESR give a free zero.

In current-mode control the inductor current is regulated inside the loop, which removes the second pole, leaving a first-order plant with a pole at 1 over (2 pi R L C) , so it's much easier to compensate.
But then the compensator gain, C and the slope compensation interact. Practically, I stay in the datasheet's L and C window and verify with a loop measurement."
